chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Buying a property is exciting. But a few classic mistakes, almost always avoidable, can cost you thousands of dollars, sometimes ten thousand and more. The good news: they are known, predictable, and this guide shows you exactly how to avoid them.

Each chapter breaks down a common mistake: why people make it, what it costs, and the simple reflex that protects you from it. At the end, an action plan and a quiz to anchor it all.

Use the "My notes" section after each chapter to spot whether you are at risk, and to correct course before it is too late.

chapters.title: Mistake #1 — Shopping without a real pre-approval
chapters.objective: Understand why buying without a solid pre-approval leads to overpaying or disappointment.
chapters.html:
Understand why buying without a solid pre-approval leads to overpaying or disappointment.

The mistake: visiting properties, falling in love, then discovering that the financing does not follow, or worse, committing beyond your means. Without a pre-approval, you know neither your real amount, nor your guaranteed rate, nor your room to manoeuvre.

What it costs

  • A dream home lost to a pre-approved buyer (in a fast market).
  • A purchase above your real capacity, revealed too late, with suffocating payments.
  • Weeks wasted visiting in the wrong price range.

The reflex that protects you

Get a pre-approval (confirmed amount + guaranteed rate for 90 to 120 days) BEFORE you shop. Remember that the lender qualifies your file at a "qualifying" rate higher than the actual rate (the stress test): the amount may be more conservative than hoped, but it is your safety ceiling.

Émilie's tip

A pre-approval is not paperwork: it is your negotiating power. At an equal price, a seller almost always chooses the offer with the strongest financing.

chapters.title: Mistake #2 — Underestimating the "invisible" costs
chapters.objective: Budget for all the purchase costs, not just the down payment and the mortgage.
chapters.html:
Budget for all the purchase costs, not just the down payment and the mortgage.

The mistake: calculating the down payment and the monthly payment, then being caught off guard by a pile of very real fees. Added together, they often exceed $10,000.

The costs to plan for

  • Welcome Tax (transfer duties): a few thousand dollars, payable after the purchase.
  • Notary fees.
  • Pre-purchase inspection and, if needed, specialized assessments.
  • Adjustments at the notary (taxes already paid by the seller, heating oil, condo).
  • Home insurance, moving, first repairs and a maintenance reserve (~1%/year of the value).

None of these items is optional or surprising in itself: it is forgetting them that costs dearly, in stress and in last-minute credit-card debt.

Émilie's tip

As soon as you have your pre-approval, ask for a written estimate of ALL the closing costs for your price range, Welcome Tax included. You budget for the whole purchase, not just the entry.

chapters.title: Mistake #3 — Rushing (or skipping) the inspection
chapters.objective: Make the inspection a real protection, not a formality.
chapters.html:
Make the inspection a real protection, not a formality.

The mistake: giving up the inspection to make your offer more "attractive" in a tight market, or picking the first inspector who comes along without reading the report. An undetected structural defect, foundation, roof, drain, pyrite, can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

The reflex that protects you

  • Make the promise to purchase conditional on an inspection by a recognized professional.
  • Go along with the inspector and ask questions; read the report in full.
  • In Québec, watch for the local issues: clay soils, pyrite/pyrrhotite, French drain, buried tank, vermiculite.

A detected problem becomes a lever: renegotiate the price, require corrections, or withdraw. That is exactly what the inspection condition allows.

Émilie's tip

Never give up the inspection just to "win" an offer. The house you land without an inspection can become the most expensive of your life.

chapters.title: Mistake #4 — Letting emotion drive the offer
chapters.objective: Keep a cool head, especially in a multiple-offer situation.
chapters.html:
Keep a cool head, especially in a multiple-offer situation.

The mistake: overbidding on a wave of emotion, dropping conditions out of fear of losing, or exceeding your limit "just this once." In a multiple-offer market, adrenaline pushes you to pay too much for the wrong reason.

The reflex that protects you

  • Set your absolute maximum price in advance, the one you are comfortable with, not just your pre-approval.
  • Offer based on a comparative market analysis (recent similar sales), not a gut feeling.
  • Remember there will be other properties: none is so unique that it is worth ruining your plan.

A "clean" offer (reasonable conditions, dates suited to the seller, solid financing) often wins without being the highest.

Émilie's tip

Write your ceiling price on a piece of paper before the negotiation, and commit to not exceeding it. Your future self will thank you.

chapters.title: Mistake #5 — Neglecting the neighbourhood, resale and documents
chapters.objective: Think beyond the crush: location, future value and documentary checks.
chapters.html:
Think beyond the crush: location, future value and documentary checks.

The mistake: buying for the decor and forgetting what really drives value, the location, the resale, and (for a condo) the financial health of the co-ownership.

The reflex that protects you

  • Assess the neighbourhood as an investment: transit, schools, services, noise, projects, resale.
  • For a condo, review the declaration of co-ownership, the contingency fund, the budget and the minutes: an underfunded fund signals special assessments.
  • Have the certificate of location and the seller's declaration reviewed before finalizing.

You never renovate a location or a neighbourhood: they are what protect your investment on resale day.

Émilie's tip

Always ask yourself the resale question on the day you buy. What holds you back today (a busy street, a poorly managed condo) will also hold back your future buyer.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Check that I have an up-to-date pre-approval.
  2. Get a written estimate of my total closing costs.

Within 30 days

  1. Choose a recognized inspector and plan for the inspection condition.
  2. Write down my absolute ceiling price and my list of neighbourhood criteria.

Then

  1. Book a free consultation with Émilie to validate my offer strategy.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Pre-approval: confirmed amount + guaranteed rate, often 90 to 120 days.
  • Closing costs: Welcome Tax, notary, inspection, adjustments, insurance.
  • Inspection condition: an exit and a negotiating lever.
  • Contingency fund: a co-ownership's collective savings for major work.
  • Comparative market analysis: recent sales of similar properties used to set the price.

qcm.q: The best protection against overpaying is:
options: B) A solid pre-approval before shopping
C) Always offering the asking price
qcm.explanation: The pre-approval sets your ceiling and makes your offers credible (mistake #1).

qcm.q: The "invisible" costs of a purchase can easily exceed:
options: D) Nothing, it's all in the mortgage
qcm.explanation: Welcome Tax, notary, inspection, adjustments and insurance add up (mistake #2).

qcm.q: Giving up the inspection to "win" an offer is risky because:
options: B) An undetected hidden defect can cost a great deal
qcm.explanation: The inspection is your protection against structural defects (mistake #3).

qcm.q: In a multiple-offer situation, the most important thing is to:
options: B) Exceed your budget to win
C) Set a ceiling price in advance and stick to it
qcm.explanation: You decide your limit calmly so as not to overbid on emotion (mistake #4).

options: B) With no conditions at all
C) With reasonable conditions, suitable dates and solid financing
qcm.explanation: It reassures the seller as much as the amount does (mistake #4).

qcm.q: For a condo, an essential document to review is:
options: B) The contingency fund and the minutes
C) The colour of the walls
qcm.explanation: An underfunded fund signals special assessments (mistake #5).

qcm.q: What you can never renovate is:
options: B) The location and the neighbourhood
qcm.explanation: The location largely determines value and resale (mistake #5).

options: B) Every month with the mortgage
C) After the purchase, in one municipal payment
qcm.explanation: It is a municipal transfer duty payable after the transaction (mistake #2).

qcm.q: The offer price should be based on:
options: A) The emotion of the moment
B) A comparative analysis of recent sales

qcm.q: The recommended maintenance reserve is about:
options: B) 1% of the value per year
qcm.explanation: About 1%/year covers roof, furnace, water heater, etc. (mistake #2).

qcm.q: The inspection condition notably allows you to:
options: B) Renegotiate, require corrections or withdraw
qcm.explanation: It is a real lever when a problem is detected (mistake #3).
